name: Cimetidine for acne
lead: Cimetidine is a histamine H2 receptor antagonist developed at Smith, Kline & French in the 1970s to reduce stomach acid, and it is sold in many countries for ulcers and heartburn.[1] Because it has a weak ability to block androgen receptors at high doses, it has occasionally been tried as an off-label treatment for acne, both by mouth and as a topical lotion.[1]

The published evidence on acne is small and dated. A 1979 Lancet report and a 1980 Lancet paper titled "Lack of effect of cimetidine in acne" are among the early items,[2][3] and a 1986 German-language pilot study of a 2% topical lotion in ten patients reported generally good clinical results, with comedones responding best and pustules hardly reduced.[4] Wikipedia describes its androgen-blocking effect as too weak to help much with acne or hirsutism, and the drug is not recommended for those uses.[1]
infobox: Oral; topical lotion tested in a small study

paras: The established uses of cimetidine are duodenal and gastric ulcers, gastroesophageal reflux disease and heartburn.[1] Use in acne is off-label and is not part of standard acne treatment as described in the sources reviewed here.[1]

Cimetidine blocks H2 receptors in the stomach and also inhibits several cytochrome P450 enzymes, which accounts for many drug interactions.[1] It weakly antagonizes the androgen receptor, but only at high doses, which is the basis of the proposal that it could reduce androgen-driven sebum and acne.[1] It can also raise estrogen levels by inhibiting estradiol metabolism.[1]

Published human data on acne are sparse and old. Lancet carried a 1979 item titled "Cimetidine in acne" and a 1980 paper titled "Lack of effect of cimetidine in acne."[2][3] In a 1986 pilot study in the Zeitschrift fur Hautkrankheiten, ten patients with papulopustular and comedonal acne applied a 2% cimetidine lotion twice daily for an average of 13 weeks; the authors reported generally good clinical success, best for comedones and then papules, little reduction of pustules, and no significant reduction in sebum excretion rate.[4] The study was uncontrolled and small.

Common effects of oral cimetidine are usually mild and include diarrhea, rash, dizziness, fatigue and constipation.[1] Gynecomastia is rare at usual doses but more likely at high doses, and sexual dysfunction and reduced sperm count have been reported.[1] Liver enzyme elevations are common but usually transient.[1]

card.summary: An old stomach-acid drug with weak antiandrogen activity that was tried for acne decades ago, with little supporting evidence.
card.note: Inhibits many drug-metabolizing enzymes; acne evidence is limited to small, dated studies.

quick.overview:
Cimetidine is an H2 blocker used for ulcers and heartburn. A few studies in the late 1970s and 1980s looked at it for acne because it can weakly block androgen receptors.

One small topical study reported generally good results in ten patients, while a 1980 Lancet paper reported no effect of the oral drug. No modern trials were found.
quick.mechanism: It blocks stomach H2 receptors and, at high doses, weakly blocks androgen receptors. It also inhibits liver enzymes and can raise estrogen levels.
quick.risks: Usually mild effects such as diarrhea and dizziness; gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction at higher doses; many drug interactions. Acne use is off-label.
